codex.worst_flaw: Not launchable as written: the records-only audit cannot distinguish a critical safety check that was actually performed from one that was merely marked complete.

codex.worst_flaw: Only reward-eligible groups get quality audits, so the pilot cannot separate the effect of the reward from extra oversight or tell whether faster reviews come at the expense of quality.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not ready to launch because the pilot never validates that its event-based score can distinguish useful reviews from rubber stamps, so token approvals could trigger a payout.

claude.worst_flaw: Every ready PR has the same eight-working-hour deadline, but the design cannot tell from events whether a review was useful. holistic.reason: Fixes the real bottleneck first (protected time, ownership, specialist routing), avoids individual scoring, and has clear exit criteria and gaming safeguards, but the team lunch is a weak draw, the private confirmations are low-visibility, and the heavy measurement rules and sampling overhead risk engineers seeing it as process burden.

claude.worst_flaw: The audit and learning setup is thin. codex.worst_flaw: With only one work group per condition in the sole concurrent comparison, the pilot cannot reliably distinguish the reward’s effect from differences in PR complexity, staffing, or shared reviewers.

holistic.reason: Fixes the queue first, uses a modest non-cash reward, aggregate-only data and anti-gaming checks, with a clear stop rule, but its dense mechanics and one-hour reward may feel low-salience and complex to sceptical engineers.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not launch-ready: the run-in sets no pass criterion for anonymous matching accuracy across shifts, so the 30-opportunity minimum cannot establish that the payout metric is reliable.

claude.worst_flaw: The documentation-coverage metric depends on observers matching anonymous kiosk records to observed moments without identity linkage, and the design never specifies how that match can be made reliably. holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous on safety, data integrity and workflow fixes with clear pause rules, but the milestone reward and audit-gated launch conditions are complex and low-salience for nurses, and sustained change depends on the kiosk becoming the default route.

codex.worst_flaw: Do not launch the reward as written: the record checks cannot detect plausible fabricated entries or whether nurses stop logging after the first credited entry, and the monthly hygiene audit cannot reliably catch resulting harm before payout.

holistic.reason: Unusually rigorous: fixes workflow first, rewards documentation rather than volume, separates adoption from independent audits, and has clear safety pause triggers, but the one-meal ward-level reward is modest and passive, so awareness and motivation may be low, and the lasting effect depends on the workflow becoming the default.

claude.worst_flaw: The design credits one valid kiosk entry per nurse-shift, so even a perfect score does not show that hand-hygiene moments were logged as asked or that hygiene improved, and it adds no individual-level check that logging matches the moments that actually happened.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not launchable as written because neither the kiosk record checks nor the separate compliance audits can detect a plausible entry for a hand-hygiene moment that never occurred.

holistic.reason: Careful, safety-first design that fixes workflow friction, avoids perverse incentives, and has clear pause rules and a sunset plan, but a ward-level catered meal is a weak, diffuse motivator that nurses may barely notice, and the main driver of lasting use is the easier kiosk workflow rather than the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not launch-ready because the design does not specify how 10 weekly audits will yield a reliable quality-adjusted score for each team's payout.

claude.worst_flaw: The two-wave comparison runs over only two weeks, with roughly 30 agents and a handful of teams in each wave, and gives no uncertainty or sample-size rule, so it cannot reliably isolate what the reward adds; some 'useful' credit also relies on a link-relevance audit of 10 tickets a week, which is too small a sample to catch agents who link marginally relevant articles.

holistic.reason: Rigorous, fair design that fixes the workflow first, uses team rather than individual rewards, protects CSAT, and includes audits and a clean stop rule, but the modest 30-minute team reward and heavy process complexity may limit motivation and awareness.

codex.worst_flaw: The flat 35% payout threshold is not calibrated to queue baselines, ticket volume, or case mix, so equally diligent teams can have materially different chances of earning the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The staggered team comparison has too few teams for a reliable estimate, with no planned sample size, uncertainty handling or cost and harm decision thresholds, so it cannot credibly isolate what the prize adds beyond the workflow fixes.

holistic.reason: Strong on workflow fixes, audit, and harm safeguards with a smart staggered design, but the team-level 30-minute break is a weak, diffuse prize, setup and audit overhead is heavy for a 60-person org, and the 35% threshold plus two-week delay may blunt employee motivation.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not launchable as written because its fixed 35% threshold counts tickets that genuinely warrant no article as misses, penalizing teams for their case mix and encouraging filler links.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no staffed appeal process or replayable record of events and rule versions, and every team gets the same 35% target and audit no matter its queue mix, number of tickets or how few tickets it gets; with only a handful of teams in the paired pilot, it also never says how uncertain the result will be.

holistic.reason: It fixes closeout friction first, protects CSAT and SLA, guards against filler links with weekly audits, and uses a randomized staggered rollout, but a reward of one 30-minute break is modest, the pilot has heavy design and audit overhead, and only 35% coverage is required with no individual incentive to drive effort.
